newsitem.title: USA: U.S. prepares to train African peacekeepers.
newsitem.headline: U.S. prepares to train African peacekeepers.

text.p: The United States is preparing to provide training and equipment to several African countries that have agreed to take part in a proposed African peacekeeping force, the U.S. State Department said on Monday.

It gave no dates and did not name specific countries, but the Washington Post said on Monday that teams of U.S. army Green Berets from Fort Bragg, North Carolina, would go to Uganda and Senegal next month to begin training battalion-size units.
Training would also be carried out in Tunisia, Ethiopia, Mali and Malawi later this year and in Ghana next year, the newspaper said, quoting U.S. administration officials.

Washington has been promoting since last year what it calls an African Crisis Response Initiative aimed at dealing with crises like the genocide that erupted in Rwanda in 1994, but with minimal involvement by non-African powers.
"We are preparing to provide training and supplemental equipment to several participating African militaries," said State Department spokesman John Dinger.

"The training and the equipment will be limited to what's required to participate in peacekeeping and humanitarian missions," he told reporters, adding that the equipment involved would be mostly for communications.
Dinger said American troops would be involved in training and logistics, but there was no plan at present for them to take part in any peacekeeping operations.
"The whole point of this is to decrease reliance on outside intervention and provide an African ability to respond to requirements for humanitarian peacekeeping," he said.
Dinger noted that the United States, Britain and France had agreed last month on principles for a joint effort on African peacekeeping.
"So our objective is to join with France, the U.K. and others to move this initiative forward as quickly and coherently as possible," he said.

The Washington Post said there would be no standing peacekeeping force and no permanent headquarters, and that the American plan was "somewhat murky" about how participating African countries would decide where to intervene.
